      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Cholesterol</span></content>

      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Cholesterol</span> is a waxy, fat-like substance that's found in all the cells in your body. Your body needs some <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> to make hormones, vitamin D, and substances that help you digest foods. Your body makes all the <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> it needs. <span class="qt1">Cholesterol</span> is also found in foods from animal sources, such as egg yolks, meat, and cheese.</p><p>If you have too much <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> in your blood, it can combine with other substances in the blood to form plaque. Plaque sticks to the walls of your arteries. This buildup of plaque is known as atherosclerosis. It can lead to coronary artery disease, a condition in which your coronary arteries become narrow or even blocked.</p>What are HDL, LDL, and VLDL?<p>HDL, LDL, and VLDL are lipoproteins. They are a combination of fat (lipid) and protein. The lipids need to be attached to the proteins so they can move through the blood. Different types of lipoproteins have different purposes:</p><ul><li>HDL stands for high-density lipoprotein. It is sometimes called "good" <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> because it helps your body get rid of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.  It carries <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> from other parts of your body back to your liver. Your liver then removes the <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> from your body.</li><li>LDL stands for low-density lipoprotein. It is sometimes called "bad" <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> because a high LDL level leads to the buildup of plaque in your arteries.</li><li>VLDL stands for very low-density lipoprotein. Some people also call VLDL a "bad" <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> because it too contributes to the buildup of plaque in your arteries. But VLDL and LDL are different; VLDL mainly carries triglycerides and LDL mainly carries <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.</li></ul>What causes high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>?<p>The most common cause of high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> is an unhealthy lifestyle. This can include:</p><ul><li>Unhealthy eating habits, such as eating lots of saturated fats. These fats are found in red meats, full-fat dairy products, chocolate, some baked goods, and many deep-fried and processed foods.  Eating too much saturated fat can raise your LDL (bad) <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.</li><li>Lack of physical activity, with lots of sitting and little exercise. This lowers your HDL (good) <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.</li><li>Smoking, which lowers HDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>, especially in women. It also raises your LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.</li><li>Stress, which may raise levels of certain hormones such as corticosteroids. These can cause your body to make more <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.</li><li>Drinking too much alcohol, which can raise your total <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> level.</li></ul><p>Genetics may also cause people to have high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. For example, familial <span class="qt0">hypercholesterolemia</span> (FH) is an inherited condition that causes very high levels of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> in the blood. Other medical conditions and certain medicines may also raise LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> levels or lower HDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> levels.</p>What can raise my risk of high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>?<p>A variety of things can raise your risk of high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>:</p><ul><li>Age. Your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> levels tend to rise as you get older. Even though it is less common, younger people, including children and teens, can also have high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.</li><li>Sex. Between ages 20 and 39, men have a greater risk of high total <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> than women. But after menopause, a woman's risk goes up. This happens because menopause lowers levels of female hormones that may protect against high blood <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.</li><li>Family history. High blood <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> can run in families.</li><li>Other health conditions. Conditions such as diabetes, chronic kidney disease, HIV, and lupus can raise your risk of high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.
</li><li>Medicines. Certain medicines can raise your level of LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> or lower your level of HDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>, including:
  <ul><li>Steroids</li><li>Some chemotherapy medicines</li><li>Medicines taken after an organ transplant</li><li>Medicines for certain heart conditions</li><li>Certain acne medicines</li></ul>
</li><li>Race or ethnicity. People from certain racial or ethnic groups may have an increased risk of high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. For example, Asian Americans are more likely to have high levels of LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> than other groups. And non-Hispanic White people are more likely than other groups to have high levels of total <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.</li><li>Weight. Being overweight or having obesity raises your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> level.</li></ul>What other health problems can high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> cause?<p>Undiagnosed or untreated high blood <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> can lead to serious health problems:</p><ul><li>If you have large deposits of plaque in your arteries, an area of plaque can rupture (break open). This can cause a blood clot to form on the surface of the plaque. If the clot becomes large enough, it can mostly or completely block blood flow in a coronary artery.</li><li>If the flow of oxygen-rich blood to your heart muscle is reduced or blocked, it can cause angina (chest pain) or a heart attack.</li><li>Plaque also can build up in other arteries in your body, including the arteries that bring oxygen-rich blood to your brain and limbs. This can lead to problems such as carotid artery disease, stroke, and peripheral arterial disease.</li></ul>How is high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> diagnosed?<p>There are usually no signs or symptoms that you have high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. A blood test can measure your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> levels. When and how often you should get this test depends on your age, risk factors, and family history.  The general recommendations are:</p><p>For people who are age 19 or younger:</p><ul><li>The first test should be between ages 9 to 11</li><li>Children should have the test again every 5 years</li><li>Some children may have this test starting at age 2 if there is a family history of high blood <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>, heart attack, or stroke</li></ul><p>For people who are ages 20 to 65:</p><ul><li>Younger adults should have the test every 5 years</li><li>Men ages 45 to 65 and women ages 55 to 65 should have it every 1 to 2 years</li></ul><p>For people over age 65:</p><ul><li>They should be tested every year</li></ul>How can I lower my <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>?<p>You can lower your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> through heart-healthy lifestyle changes. They include a heart-healthy eating plan, weight management, and regular physical activity.</p><p>If the lifestyle changes alone do not lower your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> enough, you may also need to take medicines. There are several types of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>-lowering medicines available, including statins. If you take medicines to lower your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>, you still should continue with the lifestyle changes.</p><p>Some people with familial <span class="qt0">hypercholesterolemia</span> (FH) may receive a treatment called lipoprotein apheresis. This treatment uses a filtering machine to remove LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> from the blood. Then the machine returns the rest of the blood back to the person.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Cholesterol</span> Levels: What You Need to Know</content>

      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Cholesterol</span> is a waxy, fat-like substance that's found in all the cells in your body. Your body needs some <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> to work properly. But if you have too much of it in your blood, it can stick to the walls of your arteries and narrow or even block them. This puts you at risk of coronary artery disease and other heart diseases.</p>How do you measure <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> levels?<p>A blood test called a lipoprotein or lipid panel can measure your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> levels. Before the test, you'll usually need to fast (not eat or drink anything but water) for 9 to 12 hours. Follow the instructions your health care provider gives you.</p><p>The test gives information about your:</p><ul><li>Total <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. This is a measure of the total amount of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> in your blood. It includes both low-density lipoprotein (LDL) <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.</li><li>LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. LDL is often called "bad" <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> because it is the main source of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> buildup and blockage in the arteries.</li><li>HDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. HDL is often called "good" <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> because it helps remove <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> from your arteries.</li><li>Non-HDL. This number is your total <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> minus your HDL. Your non-HDL includes LDL and other types of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> such as VLDL (very-low-density lipoprotein). It gives a better picture of all the "bad" types of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> that can raise your heart risk.</li><li>Triglycerides. This is another type of fat in your blood that can raise your risk of heart disease, especially in women.</li></ul>What do my <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> numbers mean?<p><span class="qt1">Cholesterol</span> numbers are measured in milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL). Talk with your provider about what your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> numbers should be. The numbers that are best for you may depend on your age, race, blood pressure, weight, family history, and more. However, here are some general guidelines showing the desirable levels (levels that are healthy for most people):</p><p>Anyone age 19 or younger:</p>Type of CholesterolHealthy LevelTotal CholesterolLess than 170 mg/dLNon-HDLLess than 120 mg/dLLDLLess than 110 mg/dLHDLMore than 45mg/dL<p>Men age 20 or older:</p>Type of CholesterolHealthy LevelTotal CholesterolLess than 200 mg/dLNon-HDLLess than 130 mg/dLLDLLess than 100 mg/dLHDLGreater than or equal to 60 mg/dL is best.Levels less than 40 mg/dL are considered low.<p>Women age 20 or older:</p>Type of CholesterolHealthy LevelTotal CholesterolLess than 200 mg/dLNon-HDLLess than 130 mg/dLLDLLess than 100 mg/dLHDLGreater than or equal to 60 mg/dL is best.Levels less than 50 mg/dL are considered low.<p>Triglycerides are not a type of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>, but they are also measured in this test.  A normal triglyceride level is below 150 mg/dL. You might need treatment if you have triglyceride levels that are borderline high (150-199 mg/dL) or high (200 mg/dL or more).</p>What are risk-based LDL goals?<p>If you have heart disease, or your provider thinks you might be at higher risk, they may use your LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> level to help you set goals for your LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> levels.</p><p>Your provider may use a new risk estimator tool called PREVENT, which stands for Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease EVENTs, to guide these goals and estimate your risk of heart disease. It looks at factors like your age, health history, and family history, and puts you in a risk group.</p><p>LDL goal by risk level</p>Risk levelHealthy LDL LevelLow or borderline risk100 mg/dL or belowHigh risk of future heart attack or stroke70 mg/dL or belowAlready have heart disease70 mg/dL or belowAlready have heart disease and are at very high risk55 mg/dL or belowHow often should I get a <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> test?<p>When and how often you should get a <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> test depends on your age, risk factors, and family history. The general recommendations are:</p><p>For people who are age 21 or younger:</p><ul><li>Children should be screened at least once between ages 9 to 11 and again once between ages 17 and 21</li><li>Some children may have this test starting at age 2 if there is a family history of high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>,heart attack, orstroke</li></ul><p>For people who are ages 21 to 65:</p><ul><li>Younger adults should have the test every 5 years</li><li>Men ages 45 to 65 and women ages 55 to 65 should have it every 1 to 2 years</li></ul><p>For people older than 65:</p><ul><li>They should be tested every year</li></ul><p>Additional testing may include:</p><ul><li>A lipoprotein(a) blood test once as an adult, and an apolipoprotein B or "apo B" test if you have certain health conditions. These special blood tests help your provider understand your heart risk.</li><li>A coronary calcium scan may be done to help determine if you need <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> medicines. This is animaging testwhich checks to see if you have calcium built up in your heart arteries.</li></ul>What affects my <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> levels?<p>Many factors can affect your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> levels. Some of them are things you can change:</p><ul><li>Diet. Saturatedfatand <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> in the food you eat make your blood <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> level rise. Saturated fat is the main problem, but <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> in foods also matters. Reducing the amount of saturated fat in your diet helps lower your blood <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> level. Foods that have high levels of saturated fats include red meats, full-fat dairy products, chocolate, some baked goods, and many deep-fried and processed foods.</li><li>Weight. Being overweight or havingobesityare risk factors for heart disease. They also tend to increase your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. If you have high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> and are overweight, it's recommended that you lose at least 5% of your body weight, which would be 10 pounds for a 200-pound person.</li><li>Lack of physical activity. Not being physically active is a risk factor for heart disease.</li><li>Smoking.Cigarette smokinglowers your HDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. Since HDL helps to remove <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> from your arteries, having a lower HDL level can contribute to a higher <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> level.</li></ul><p>Some factors that you cannot change can also affect your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> levels, such as</p><ul><li>Age. Your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> levels tend to rise as you get older. Even though it is less common, younger people, includingchildren and teens, can also have high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.</li><li>Sex. Between ages 20 and 39, men have a greater risk of high total <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> than women. But aftermenopause, a woman's risk goes up. This happens because menopause lowers levels of female hormones that may protect against high blood <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.</li><li>Family history. Your genes partly determine how much <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> your body makes. High <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> can run in families.</li><li>Ethnicity. Your ethnicity may increase your risk of high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.</li></ul>How can I lower my <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>?<p>You canlower your cholesterolthrough heart-healthy lifestyle changes: They include aheart-healthy eating plan,weight management, andregular physical activity.</p><p>If the lifestyle changes alone do not lower your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> enough, you may also need to take medicines. There are several types ofcholesterol-lowering drugsavailable, includingstatins. You may need a statin if you:</p><ul><li>Are age 30 or older and have an LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> of 160 mg/dL or higher</li><li>Have a strong family history of heart disease</li></ul><p>If you take medicines to lower your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>, you still should continue with the lifestyle changes.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title">How to Lower <span class="qt1">Cholesterol</span> with Diet</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Low <span class="qt1">Cholesterol</span> Diet</content>
      <content name="altTitle">TLC Diet</content>

      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Cholesterol</span> is a waxy, fat-like substance that's found in all the cells in your body. Your body needs some <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> to work properly. But if you have too much of it in your blood, it can stick to the walls of your arteries and narrow or even block them. This puts you at risk for coronary artery disease and other heart diseases.</p><p><span class="qt1">Cholesterol</span> is made by your liver. It travels through the blood on proteins called lipoproteins. One type of lipoprotein, LDL, is sometimes called the "bad" <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. A high LDL level leads to a buildup of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> in your arteries. Another type, HDL, is sometimes called the "good" <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. It carries <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> from other parts of your body back to your liver. Then your liver removes the <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> from your body.</p>What are the treatments for high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>?<p>The main treatments for high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> are heart-healthy lifestyle changes and medicines. The lifestyle changes include healthy eating, weight management, and regular physical activity.</p>How can I lower <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> with diet?<p>Heart-healthy lifestyle changes include a diet to lower your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. The DASH eating plan is one example. Another is the Therapeutic Lifestyle Changes (TLC) diet, which recommends that you:</p><p>Choose healthier fats.You should limit both total fat and saturated fat. No more than 25 to 35% of your daily calories should come from dietary fats, and less than 7% of your daily calories should come from saturated fat. Depending upon how many calories you eat per day, here are the maximum amounts of saturated fats that you should eat:</p>Calories per DaySaturated Fat1,2008 grams1,50010 grams2,00013 grams2,50017 grams<p>Saturated fat is a bad fat because it raises your LDL (bad <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>) level more than anything else in your diet. It is found in some meats, dairy products, chocolate, baked goods, and deep-fried and processed foods.</p><p>Instead of saturated fats, switch to foods with healthier fats, such as lean meat, nuts, and unsaturated oils like canola, olive, and safflower oils.</p><p>Limit foods with <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. If you are trying to lower your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>, you should have less than 200 mg a day of <span class="qt1">cholesterol. Cholesterol</span> is in foods from animals, such as liver and other organ meats, egg yolks, shrimp, and whole milk dairy products.</p><p>Eat plenty of soluble fiber. Soluble fiber helps prevent your digestive tract from absorbing <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. You should try to get 10 to 25 grams of it per day. Foods that are high in soluble fiber include:</p><ul><li>Whole-grain cereals such as oatmeal and oat bran</li><li>Fruits such as apples, bananas, oranges, pears, and prunes</li><li>Legumes such as kidney beans, lentils, chickpeas, black-eyed peas, and lima beans</li></ul><p>Eat lots of fruits and vegetables. They are important sources of vitamins, fiber, and other nutrients.</p><p>Increase plant stanols and sterols in your diet.These are substances that also help prevent your digestive tract from absorbing <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. You should try to get 2 grams of them per day. They can be found in whole grains, nuts, legumes, and oils, such as olive oil and avocado oil. They are also added to some foods, such as certain types of orange juice, margarine, and bread.</p><p>Eat foods that are high in omega-3 fatty acids. These special fats can lower LDL and triglyceride levels. They can also help control blood pressure and may lower your risk of heart rhythm problems. If you have heart disease, they may lower your risk of heart attack.  Omega-3 fatty acids can be found in:</p><ul><li>Fish such as salmon, tuna (canned or fresh), and mackerel. Most people should try to eat these fish two times a week. But if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, you should avoid fish that could be high in mercury, such as mackerel.</li><li>Plant sources such as walnuts, flaxseed, chia seeds, and canola and soybean oils. But they have smaller amounts of omega-3 acids than the fish sources.</li><li>Fortified foods, such as certain brands of eggs, yogurt, juices, milk, soy beverages, and infant formulas.</li></ul><p>Limit salt. You should try to limit the amount of sodium (salt) that you eat to no more than 2,300 milligrams (about 1 teaspoon of salt) a day. That includes all the sodium you eat, whether it's added in cooking, used at the table, or already present in food products. Limiting salt won't lower your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>, but it can lower your risk of heart diseases by helping to lower your blood pressure. You can reduce your sodium by instead choosing low-salt and "no added salt" foods and seasonings at the table or while cooking.</p><p>Limit alcohol. Alcohol adds extra calories, which can lead to weight gain. Being overweight can raise your LDL level and lower your HDL level. Too much alcohol can also increase your risk of heart diseases because it can raise your blood pressure and triglyceride level. It's best not to drink, but if you do: </p><ul><li>Have no more than 2 drinks per day if you are a man</li><li>Have no more than 1 drink per day if you are a woman</li></ul><p>Nutrition labels can help you figure out how much fat, saturated fat, <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>, fiber, and sodium is in the foods that you buy. This can help you eat healthier and lower your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Cholesterol</span> is a waxy, fat-like substance that's found in all the cells in your body. Your body needs some <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> to work properly.  But if you have too much of it in your blood, it can stick to the walls of your arteries and narrow or even block them. This puts you at risk for coronary artery disease and other heart diseases.</p><p><span class="qt1">Cholesterol</span> is made by your liver. It travels through the blood on proteins called lipoproteins. One type of lipoprotein, LDL, is sometimes called the "bad" <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. A high LDL level leads to a buildup of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> in your arteries. Another type, HDL, is sometimes called the "good" <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. It carries <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> from other parts of your body back to your liver. Then your liver removes the <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> from your body.</p>What are the treatments for high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>?<p>If you have high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>, lifestyle changes can help you lower your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> levels. But sometimes the lifestyle changes are not enough, and you need to take <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> medicines. But you should still continue with the lifestyle changes even though you are taking medicines.</p>Who needs <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> medicines?<p>Your health care provider may prescribe <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> medicines for you if:</p><ul><li>You have already had a heart attack or stroke, or you have peripheral arterial disease</li><li>Your LDL (bad) <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> level is 190 mg/dL or higher</li><li>You are 40-75 years old, you have diabetes, and your LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> level is 70 mg/dL or higher</li><li>You are 40-75 years old, you have a high risk of developing heart disease or stroke, and your LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> level is 70 mg/dL or higher</li></ul>What are the different types of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> medicines?<p>There are several types of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>-lowering drugs available, including:</p><ul><li>Statins. They reduce the amount of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> made in the liver. They also increase your liver's ability to remove LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> that is already in the blood. Statins are the most common medicines used to treat high <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.</li><li>Bile acid sequestrants.  They keep bile acids, which digest fats and oils, from being absorbed into the body.  But your body needs bile acids, so your liver will make more of them. It makes them by breaking down LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>, so this helps lower your LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. Your provider may prescribe these medicines if you cannot take statins or if statins alone are not lowering your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> enough.</li><li><span class="qt1">Cholesterol</span> absorption inhibitors.  They block how <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> is absorbed into the body. They are also used if you cannot take statins or if statins alone are not lowering your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> enough.</li><li>Nicotinic acid (niacin).  It is a type of B vitamin. It reduces the amount of fats made by your liver, so it lowers your LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> and triglycerides. Niacin also raises HDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. Even though you can buy niacin without a prescription, you should talk to your provider before taking it to lower your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>. High doses of niacin can cause serious side effects.</li><li>PCSK9 inhibitors. They block a protein called PCSK9. This helps your liver remove and clear LDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> from your blood. Your provider may prescribe a PCSK9 inhibitor and a statin if you are at high risk of complications like heart attack or stroke, or if you have familial <span class="qt0">hypercholesterolemia</span> (FH). FH is an inherited disorder that causes very high levels of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> in the blood.</li><li>Fibrates.  They lower triglycerides in several complex ways, including reducing the amount of triglycerides made by the liver. They may also help increase HDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> and may lower LDL levels a bit. If you take them with statins, it might increase the risk of side effects.</li><li>Combination medicines. They include more than one type of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>-lowering medicine. There are also combination medicines that can treat both high blood pressure and <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>.</li></ul><p>There are also a few other <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> medicines (lomitapide and mipomersen) that are only for people who have FH.</p>How does my health care provider decide which <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> medicine I should take?<p>When deciding which medicine you should take and which dose you need, your provider will consider:</p><ul><li>Your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> levels.</li><li>Your risk for heart disease and stroke.</li><li>Your age.</li><li>Any other health problems you have.</li><li>Possible side effects of the medicines. Higher doses are more likely to cause side effects, especially over time.</li></ul><p>Medicines can help control your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>, but they don't cure it. You need to keep taking your medicines and get regular <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> checks to make sure that your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> levels are in a healthy range.</p></content>

      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">High-density lipoprotein</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Cholesterol</span> is a waxy, fat-like substance that's found in all the cells in your body. Your liver makes <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>, and it is also in some foods, such as meat and dairy products. Your body needs some <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> to work properly. But having too much <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> in your blood raises your risk of coronary artery disease.</p>What are HDL and LDL?<p>HDL and LDL are two types of lipoproteins.They are a combination of fat (lipid) and protein.  The lipids need to be attached to the proteins so they can move through the blood. HDL and LDL have different purposes:</p><ul><li>HDL stands for high-density lipoproteins. It is sometimes called the "good" <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> because it carries <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> from other parts of your body back to your liver. Your liver then removes the <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> from your body.</li><li>LDL stands for low-density lipoproteins. It is sometimes called the "bad" <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> because a high LDL level leads to a buildup of <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> in your arteries.</li></ul>How do I know what my HDL level is?<p>A blood test can measure your <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> levels, including HDL. When and how often you should get this test depends on your age, risk factors, and family history.  The general recommendations are:</p><p>For people who are age 19 or younger:</p><ul><li>The first test should be between ages 9 to 11</li><li>Children should have the test again every 5 years</li><li>Some children may have this test starting at age 2 if there is a family history of high blood <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>, heart attack, or stroke</li></ul><p>For people who are age 20 or older:</p><ul><li>Younger adults should have the test every 5 years</li><li>Men ages 45 to 65 and women ages 55 to 65 should have it every 1 to 2 years</li></ul>What should my HDL level be?<p> With HDL <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span>, higher numbers are better, because a high HDL level can lower your risk for coronary artery disease and stroke. How high your HDL should be depends on your age and sex:</p>GroupHealthy HDL LevelAge 19 or youngerMore than 45mg/dlMen age 20 or olderMore than 40mg/dlWomen age 20 or olderMore than 50mg/dlHow can I raise my HDL level?<p>If your HDL level is too low, lifestyle changes may help. These changes may also help prevent other diseases and make you feel better overall:</p><ul><li>Eat a healthy diet. To raise your HDL level, you need to eat good fats instead of bad fats. This means limiting saturated fats, which include full-fat milk and cheese, high-fat meats like sausage and bacon, and foods made with butter, lard, and shortening. You should also avoid trans fats, which may be in some margarines, fried foods, and processed foods like baked goods. Instead, eat unsaturated fats, which are found in avocado, vegetable oils like olive oil, and nuts. Limit carbohydrates, especially sugar. Also try to eat more foods naturally high in fiber, such as oatmeal and beans.</li><li>Stay at a healthy weight. You can boost your HDL level by losing weight, especially if you have lots of fat around your waist.</li><li>Exercise. Getting regular exercise can raise your HDL level, as well as lower your LDL. You should try to do 30 minutes of moderate to vigorous aerobic exercise on most, if not all, days.</li><li>Avoid cigarettes.Smoking and exposure to secondhand smoke can lower your HDL level. If you are a smoker, ask your health care provider for help in finding the best way for you to quit. You should also try to avoid secondhand smoke.</li><li>Limit alcohol. Moderate alcohol may lower your HDL level, although more studies are needed to confirm that. What we do know is that too much alcohol can make you gain weight, and that lowers your HDL level.</li></ul><p>Some <span class="qt1">cholesterol</span> medicines, including certain statins, can raise your HDL level, in addition to lowering your LDL level. Health care providers don't usually prescribe medicines only to raise HDL. But if you have a low HDL and high LDL level, you might need medicine.</p>What else can affect my HDL level?<p>Taking certain medicines can lower HDL levels in some people. They include:</p><ul><li>Beta blockers, a type of blood pressure medicine</li><li>Anabolic steroids, including testosterone, a male hormone</li><li>Progestins, which are female hormones that are in some birth control pills and hormone therapy for menopause</li><li>Benzodiazepines, sedatives that are often used for anxiety and insomnia</li></ul><p>If you are taking one of these and you have a very low HDL level, ask your provider if you should continue to take them.</p><p>Diabetes can also lower your HDL level, so that gives you another reason to manage your diabetes.</p></content>
